cast: hero (you, black head, blue hoodie, NO balance ever, not in a mirror, not anywhere)
sam (best friend, black head, orange top, $212.50 orange, $210.00 after the snack, $205.00 after buying Derek lunch)
mrs. hale (teacher, $12,400 green, buys two coffees every morning, one for the janitor's cart)
maya (the quiet girl, $312 orange, draws in a notebook, shares her fries)
derek (the captain, $0.00 red pulsing, new shoes every week, spends everything trying to look rich)
mr. ellis (the janitor, $8,412,009 gold with glow, mopped the same hallway for forty years)
mrs. park (cafeteria cashier, $40 red, ticks $40 to $44 to $48, +$4 a lunch)
mr. grant (principal, $86,000 green, eats lunch alone in his office)
mom (pays the electric bill, her number drops $112, flashes red)

script.text: You are standing in the lunch line when it happens. Above the cashier's head, a number appears. $40. It floats there, soft and white, like a price tag in the air. Nobody else looks up. Nobody else can see it. You blink. The number stays. Mrs. Park hands you your tray and takes your lunch money. Her number ticks up. $40. $44. $48. Money just moved, and you watched it move. Sam elbows you in the ribs. "You okay? You look like you saw a ghost." You point up. "Above her head. The number." Sam looks. "What number?" And that's when you get it. The numbers are only for you. So, what if you could see how much money everyone has?

Here's the deal. You figure out three rules, fast. Rule one: the number is everything a person has. Cash in a wallet. Money in the bank. All of it, added up, floating over their head. Rule two: it ticks. The second money moves, the number moves. Money in, it flashes green and climbs. Money out, it flashes red and drops. Rule three: you can't see your own number. You stand in front of the bathroom mirror and look up. Nothing. No number above your head at all. File that away. You'll need it. You test rule two that night at home. Your mom pays the electric bill on her phone. One tap. Her number drops a hundred and twelve dollars in a single blink. You test it on Sam the next morning. He buys a snack. His number drops two dollars and fifty cents. Sam grins. "The emergency five stays in the shoe, though." "That's the rule."

So you run an experiment. All day, at school, you read everyone. Mrs. Hale, your teacher: $12,400. She buys two coffees every morning. One for her. One she leaves on the janitor's cart. Maya, the quiet girl: $312. She draws in a notebook all through lunch. She shares her fries with anyone who sits down. Sam: $212.50. He saves every lunch dollar. The emergency five stays in the shoe. The principal, Mr. Grant: $86,000. He eats lunch alone in his office, door closed. At the snack machine, a kid feeds in two dollars. His number ticks down, two dollars, right in front of you. You could watch anyone's money move, any time you wanted. It feels like a superpower. It feels a little bit like spying. Then Derek. The captain. New shoes every week. His dad's car in the parking lot. Everybody wants to be Derek. His number: $0.00. Zero. Not one dollar. You stare so long he notices. "What are you looking at?" "Nothing," you say. "Nice shoes." And in the hallway, between classes, you see something else. A man mopping the floor. Above his head, a number so big it doesn't fit your brain. $8,412,009. You blink. He turns the corner. Gone. You tell yourself you imagined it. Nobody has that kind of money and mops a school hallway.

This next bit is real. No one can actually see a number above your head. That's the made-up part. But the part about money and happiness? Scientists tested that. In 2010, two researchers named Kahneman and Deaton studied thousands of Americans. They found something strange. Happiness climbs as income climbs, up to about seventy-five thousand dollars a year. Then it stops. More money after that doesn't make people feel better day to day. The number keeps growing. The feeling doesn't. And in 2008, three more researchers, Dunn, Aknin, and Norton, ran a different test. They gave people money and told half of them to spend it on themselves, and half to spend it on someone else. The people who spent it on someone else felt happier. Every time. So the science says two things. Money helps, up to a point. And giving it away feels better than keeping it. But the numbers above everyone's heads don't show any of that. They only show the money.

And that's when the numbers start to cost you. Because knowing someone's number feels like power. And power is hard to put down. At lunch, Derek is showing off his new shoes again. The whole table is watching. And you say it. Out loud. In front of everyone. "Nice shoes, Derek. Too bad you've got zero dollars. $0.00." The table goes quiet. Then it laughs. Derek's face goes red. He stands up. He walks out. Sam looks at you like you just kicked a dog. "That was mean. You didn't have to say it." You feel powerful for about two seconds. Then you feel sick. Because the number was true. And it still hurt. And it doesn't stop there. First, it's small. You bet Sam five dollars that the new kid has less than a hundred. You win. It feels clever. Then it's bigger. You start checking numbers before you talk to anyone, like a price tag on a person. You catch yourself checking Maya's three hundred dollars before you decide where to sit. You sit with the big numbers. You avoid the small ones. You notice yourself doing it. You don't stop.

script.beat: 6 the mirror (you can't see your own)
script.text: That night, you stand in front of the bathroom mirror again. Still nothing above your head. You ask Sam the next day. "What do you think mine says?" Sam shrugs. "I can't see any numbers. Only you can." And it hits you. You spent a whole week ranking everyone, and you don't even know your own rank. But here's the worse part. Mrs. Hale's twelve thousand doesn't say she's kind. Maya's three hundred doesn't say she's generous. Derek's zero doesn't say he's a bad person. The numbers told you about money. You decided they meant worth.

So after school, you go back to the hallway. Mr. Ellis is there. The janitor. Mopping the same floor he's mopped for forty years. Above his head: $8,412,009. The richest person in the whole school. You were right. You didn't imagine it. He finishes mopping. He picks up the coffee Mrs. Hale left on his cart. He smiles at it, like it's a gift. You walk up to him. "Mr. Ellis. Why do you still work here?" He leans on his mop. "Somebody's got to keep the floors clean. And the kids are good company." Here's what the number doesn't say. Forty years of saving. A small inheritance from his mother that he never touched. It grew, year after year, while he just kept mopping. He has millions. And he mops floors because he likes it here. And Derek? The one everyone envies? He has zero dollars because he spends everything the second he gets it, trying to look rich. The numbers were right all along. Your reading of them was wrong.

script.beat: 8 the moral (the number never measures worth)
script.text: The next morning, you walk into school, and the numbers are still there. But this time, you look at faces first. You sit with Maya. She shares her fries. You apologize to Derek. He nods, and that's enough. At lunch, Sam does something. He takes the emergency five out of his shoe, the five he swore he'd never spend, and buys Derek lunch. "Emergency," he says. "This counts." Derek eats. Nobody laughs. That feels better than any number. Sam is already saving up a new emergency five. He doesn't even care. On your way out, you pass Mr. Ellis, still mopping. His number is still there. Eight million, four hundred and twelve thousand, and nine dollars. You don't even read it anymore. You just say, "Morning, Mr. Ellis." He says, "Morning, kid." And that's the whole thing. And you finally get it. The number never measures what a person is worth. It never did. If you could see one number above everyone's head, what would you want it to be? What would yours say? Tell us in the comments.
